note: Recommended pedagogical dependencies, not universal scientific necessities. All required edges use AND semantics. Framework alternatives and optional branches are explicit. Estimates are rough hands-on study hours, not completion promises.

nodes.title: Python essentials
nodes.summary: Values, control flow, functions, collections and files let you turn an idea into a repeatable program. Separate input, transformation and output; add a small test before growing the script.
nodes.question: Why use a dictionary instead of a list for lookup by document ID?
nodes.answer: A dictionary maps unique keys to values and offers average constant-time key lookup. A list is ordered and usually needs a scan to find a matching ID. Neither removes the need to handle missing data.
nodes.project: Write a function that counts words in three strings; test empty input and repeated words.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Write a function that counts words in three strings; test empty input and repeated words.

nodes.title: Git & reproducible work
nodes.summary: A repository records changes; a commit captures a coherent version. Keep source and small fixtures in Git, secrets and generated model weights outside it. Save the command that reproduces your result.
nodes.question: How does a commit differ from a backup of your entire laptop?
nodes.answer: A commit records tracked project files and their history. It does not automatically include ignored files, untracked files, environments or external datasets. Back those up separately.
nodes.project: Create a local repository, commit a tiny script and its test, then inspect a diff.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Create a local repository, commit a tiny script and its test, then inspect a diff.

nodes.title: Terminal & Linux basics
nodes.summary: Learn paths, working directories, processes and environment variables. PowerShell is sufficient for the supplied Windows launcher; Linux skills help when you move a static library to a Pi.
nodes.question: Why can a relative path work in one terminal and fail in another?
nodes.answer: A relative path is resolved from the current working directory. Use an explicit project directory or derive paths from the script location.
nodes.project: List a project directory, run a script from its root and explain the resulting file paths.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: List a project directory, run a script from its root and explain the resulting file paths.

nodes.title: Probability
nodes.summary: Probabilities describe uncertainty. Conditional probability changes the sample space; independent events are a special case. Simulations approximate expectations and should include a seed when reproducibility matters.
nodes.question: Is P(A given B) generally equal to P(B given A)?
nodes.answer: No. Bayes rule connects them through P(A) and P(B). Rare-event base rates can change the conclusion even when a test has high sensitivity.
nodes.project: Simulate a biased coin and compare empirical frequency with its specified probability.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Simulate a biased coin and compare empirical frequency with its specified probability.

nodes.title: Statistics & measurement
nodes.summary: Separate an estimate from uncertainty about that estimate. Training, validation and final test sets serve different purposes. Repeatedly tuning against the final test set leaks information into your choices.
nodes.question: Why does a high training score not establish generalization?
nodes.answer: The model or your choices may fit training-specific patterns. Evaluate once on held-out examples and examine sample size, uncertainty and distribution shift.
nodes.project: Split a small dataset before fitting a baseline; report both training and held-out errors.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Split a small dataset before fitting a baseline; report both training and held-out errors.

nodes.title: Linear algebra
nodes.summary: Vectors represent collections of numbers; matrices describe linear maps. Track shapes before implementing a model. A dot product is a scalar, while an outer product is a matrix.
nodes.question: What is the shape of A @ B when A is 3 by 4 and B is 4 by 2?
nodes.answer: The result is 3 by 2. The shared inner dimension must match; reversing the multiplication is not generally valid.
nodes.project: Implement a dot product and matrix multiplication for small lists; test shape mismatches.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Implement a dot product and matrix multiplication for small lists; test shape mismatches.

nodes.title: Calculus & gradients
nodes.summary: A derivative measures local sensitivity. The chain rule connects derivatives through a computation. A gradient gives sensitivities with respect to multiple parameters; gradient descent moves against it.
nodes.question: Why compare an analytic gradient with a finite-difference estimate?
nodes.answer: They are independent ways to approximate the same local derivative. Agreement at sensible step sizes helps detect implementation errors; floating-point error limits very small steps.
nodes.project: Check the derivative of a quadratic numerically and show one gradient-descent step.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Check the derivative of a quadratic numerically and show one gradient-descent step.

nodes.title: Supervised machine learning
nodes.summary: Learn a mapping from inputs to labelled targets. Begin with a simple baseline and choose a metric that fits the task. Fit preprocessing on training data only.
nodes.question: Why fit a scaler only on the training split?
nodes.answer: Using held-out distribution statistics during fitting leaks information. Reuse training-derived parameters to transform validation and test data.
nodes.project: Train a simple classifier or regressor, compare with a trivial baseline and report held-out performance.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Train a simple classifier or regressor, compare with a trivial baseline and report held-out performance.

nodes.title: Unsupervised machine learning
nodes.summary: Clustering groups examples under a chosen geometry; dimensionality reduction finds useful representations. A cluster is not automatically a true category or causal explanation.
nodes.question: Why can feature scaling change k-means clusters?
nodes.answer: Distance depends on numerical scale. A high-range feature can dominate Euclidean distances, so scaling choices change the geometry and the result.
nodes.project: Cluster a tiny two-dimensional dataset and compare assignments before and after scaling.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Cluster a tiny two-dimensional dataset and compare assignments before and after scaling.

nodes.title: Neural networks & deep learning
nodes.summary: Compose parameterized transformations and nonlinearities, define a loss, then backpropagate derivatives. Depth alone does not guarantee better generalization. Monitor validation loss and numerical stability.
nodes.question: What does backpropagation compute, and what does an optimizer do?
nodes.answer: Backpropagation computes loss gradients using the chain rule. An optimizer uses those gradients and its update rule to change parameters. These are separate operations.
nodes.project: Build a two-layer network on a toy task and test one parameter gradient.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Build a two-layer network on a toy task and test one parameter gradient.

nodes.title: PyTorch training workflow
nodes.summary: Tensors, autograd, data loaders and explicit train/evaluation modes form the training loop. Clear gradients appropriately and keep evaluation separate from parameter updates.
nodes.question: Why call zero_grad before another independent training step?
nodes.answer: Gradients accumulate by default. Clearing them prevents accidental addition across steps unless deliberate gradient accumulation is intended.
nodes.project: Train a tiny network, save a checkpoint and reproduce its evaluation predictions.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Train a tiny network, save a checkpoint and reproduce its evaluation predictions.

nodes.title: TensorFlow alternative
nodes.summary: TensorFlow and Keras provide another tensor and training ecosystem. This is an optional alternative exploration; learning both frameworks is not a prerequisite for RAG or transformers.
nodes.question: What should stay comparable when porting a model between frameworks?
nodes.answer: Data splits, preprocessing, architecture, loss, optimization settings and evaluation protocol should match. Numerical details can still produce small differences.
nodes.project: Recreate one small trained model in Keras and compare held-out predictions.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Recreate one small trained model in Keras and compare held-out predictions.

nodes.title: Text processing & documents
nodes.summary: Treat text as versioned data. Preserve document IDs, encoding, source information and boundaries. Normalization can help search but can also destroy meaningful distinctions such as code case.
nodes.question: Why retain source IDs after cleaning and chunking documents?
nodes.answer: IDs let you trace a passage to its source, update changed documents, inspect citations and avoid duplicate ingestion. Keep offsets or passage IDs too.
nodes.project: Load three UTF-8 notes into records containing stable IDs, titles and text.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Load three UTF-8 notes into records containing stable IDs, titles and text.

nodes.title: Tokenization
nodes.summary: Tokenizers map text into token IDs according to a vocabulary and encoding procedure. Tokens need not be whole words. The tokenizer and model vocabulary must agree.
nodes.question: Why is word count not the same as token count?
nodes.answer: A word can split into several subword or byte tokens; whitespace, symbols and language affect segmentation. Use the model tokenizer when measuring its context budget.
nodes.project: Compare character and word tokenizers on punctuation, Unicode and unseen words.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compare character and word tokenizers on punctuation, Unicode and unseen words.

nodes.title: Embeddings & similarity
nodes.summary: An embedding maps an item to a vector. Similarity reflects the model and training objective, not guaranteed truth. Retrieval can use pretrained embeddings without training your own model.
nodes.question: Does a high cosine similarity prove two passages say the same thing?
nodes.answer: No. It measures direction similarity in a particular representation. Negation, numbers and fine distinctions can still be wrong; evaluate retrieved passages against labelled questions.
nodes.project: Rank a few toy vectors by cosine similarity; explain zero-vector handling.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Rank a few toy vectors by cosine similarity; explain zero-vector handling.

nodes.title: Word2Vec: optional historical branch
nodes.summary: Word2Vec learns word vectors from local context prediction. Static word vectors give one representation per vocabulary entry, unlike contextual representations that depend on the surrounding text.
nodes.question: How would static and contextual embeddings handle the two meanings of bank?
nodes.answer: A static word vector shares one representation for bank. A contextual model can produce different representations for river bank and financial bank.
nodes.project: Write two ambiguous sentences and compare what static versus contextual representations can express.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Write two ambiguous sentences and compare what static versus contextual representations can express.

nodes.title: Attention & self-attention
nodes.summary: Scaled dot-product attention computes softmax(Q Kᵀ / sqrt(d_k)) V. In self-attention, queries, keys and values are derived from the same input sequence. A causal mask blocks access to future tokens.
nodes.question: If Q and K are T by d_k, what is the shape of their attention score matrix?
nodes.answer: Q K-transpose has shape T by T. Each row compares one query position with key positions. Row-wise softmax creates weights before multiplication with V.
nodes.project: Compute a two-token attention example and verify that each softmax row sums to one.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compute a two-token attention example and verify that each softmax row sums to one.

nodes.title: Multi-head attention
nodes.summary: Different learned projections create attention heads. Their outputs are concatenated and projected back into the model representation. Heads are not guaranteed to have human-interpretable roles.
nodes.question: For d_model=64 and 4 equal heads, what is each head dimension?
nodes.answer: The conventional equal-head setup uses 16 dimensions per head. Concatenating four head outputs restores 64 dimensions before the output projection.
nodes.project: Trace batch, head, sequence and feature dimensions through a four-head attention block.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Trace batch, head, sequence and feature dimensions through a four-head attention block.

nodes.title: Positional information
nodes.summary: Attention needs a way to represent order. Original transformers use positional encodings; other designs use learned positions or rotary transformations. Positional methods have different extrapolation behavior.
nodes.question: Why does a transformer need positional information?
nodes.answer: Without positional information or order-sensitive structure, self-attention alone does not encode sequence order. Position representations distinguish permutations of otherwise identical tokens.
nodes.project: Compare representations of the same tokens in two orders with and without position information.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compare representations of the same tokens in two orders with and without position information.

nodes.title: Transformer architecture
nodes.summary: Combine attention, feed-forward layers, residual connections and normalization. Encoder, decoder and encoder-decoder designs serve different objectives. A GPT-style decoder uses causal attention.
nodes.question: What prevents next-token training from seeing the target token through future positions?
nodes.answer: Inputs and targets are shifted appropriately and causal attention masks future positions. Dataset construction and masking must both avoid target leakage.
nodes.project: Draw a decoder block with tensor shapes and test a causal mask on a tiny input.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Draw a decoder block with tensor shapes and test a causal mask on a tiny input.

nodes.title: Use a local LLM
nodes.summary: Inference uses learned weights and a supplied context to generate token predictions. Sampling affects variability; it does not verify facts. Keep a fixed test prompt set and record model and settings.
nodes.question: How do context, retrieval and training differ?
nodes.answer: Context is temporary input. Retrieval selects information to supply as context. Training changes learned parameters. A long prompt does not update model weights.
nodes.project: Compare two prompts on the same local model, recording settings, latency and one failure.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compare two prompts on the same local model, recording settings, latency and one failure.

nodes.title: Safety, privacy & source boundaries
nodes.summary: Treat model outputs and retrieved documents as untrusted. Validate tool arguments in code, minimize permissions, and keep actions bounded. Prompt instructions alone cannot enforce a security boundary.
nodes.question: What should happen if a retrieved document asks the assistant to delete files?
nodes.answer: Treat it as document content, not an authorized instruction. The application should lack that tool or require independently validated authorization before any such action.
nodes.project: Add a hostile document to a retrieval fixture and verify that no tool action can execute.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Add a hostile document to a retrieval fixture and verify that no tool action can execute.

nodes.title: Evaluation & regression sets
nodes.summary: Separate retrieval metrics from answer quality. Keep answerable, unanswerable and adversarial examples, with expected sources. Reserve held-out examples to assess changes after development.
nodes.question: Can perfect retrieval recall guarantee a correct generated answer?
nodes.answer: No. The model can ignore or misread relevant evidence. Evaluate support, citation correctness, abstention and latency separately from retrieval recall.
nodes.project: Create ten answerable and five unanswerable questions; record expected sources and a baseline.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Create ten answerable and five unanswerable questions; record expected sources and a baseline.

nodes.title: RAG & keyword retrieval
nodes.summary: A RAG pipeline retrieves passages and supplies them as evidence for generation. BM25 provides a useful lexical baseline and does not require embedding training. Show evidence before trusting an answer.
nodes.question: When is RAG more appropriate than fine-tuning?
nodes.answer: RAG is useful when answers require changing or inspectable external facts. Fine-tuning adapts behavior or task performance; it is not a reliable substitute for a versioned document store.
nodes.project: Use Ask your sources to inspect four passages; record supported answers and abstentions.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Use Ask your sources to inspect four passages; record supported answers and abstentions.

nodes.title: Vector & hybrid retrieval
nodes.summary: Dense retrieval compares embeddings; lexical retrieval matches terms. Hybrid systems combine signals, often followed by reranking. Measure gains on the same questions before adding infrastructure.
nodes.question: Why retain lexical retrieval alongside embeddings?
nodes.answer: Exact identifiers and rare terms can be important. Embeddings can help paraphrases. Their strengths differ, so a measured hybrid system can improve coverage.
nodes.project: Compare lexical and embedding rankings for exact-ID and paraphrase questions; record recall at k.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compare lexical and embedding rankings for exact-ID and paraphrase questions; record recall at k.

nodes.title: Tool-using agents
nodes.summary: An agent delegates some action selection to a model. Explicit tool contracts, state, step budgets, timeouts and traces make behavior inspectable. Begin with a predictable workflow and add decisions only where needed.
nodes.question: What stops an agent from repeatedly calling a failing tool?
nodes.answer: Enforced step/time budgets, retry limits and state checks outside the model. A prompt asking it to stop is not a sufficient operational control.
nodes.project: Implement a read-only search tool with argument validation, a two-step budget and a timeout test.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Implement a read-only search tool with argument validation, a two-step budget and a timeout test.

nodes.title: Multi-agent systems & MCP
nodes.summary: Multiple agents can divide tasks but add coordination and failure modes. MCP standardizes connections to tools and resources; it does not itself create a planner or validate every tool action.
nodes.question: When would two agents be worse than one deterministic workflow?
nodes.answer: When coordination, duplicated calls or conflicting state cost more than any task specialization helps. Compare success rate, latency and trace complexity against a simpler baseline.
nodes.project: Compare one workflow with a planner/reviewer pair on fixed tasks; retain only measured improvements.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compare one workflow with a planner/reviewer pair on fixed tasks; retain only measured improvements.

nodes.title: Pretraining a tiny language model
nodes.summary: Pretraining learns an objective such as next-token prediction from a corpus. Split data carefully, estimate token and compute budgets and train a tiny example before scaling. A laptop exercise is not frontier-model training.
nodes.question: Why keep validation text separate before creating overlapping token windows?
nodes.answer: Overlapping windows can otherwise leak nearly identical text across splits, making validation loss too optimistic. Split at meaningful source boundaries before windowing.
nodes.project: Train or specify a tiny decoder experiment with data splits, loss curve and a saved checkpoint.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Train or specify a tiny decoder experiment with data splits, loss curve and a saved checkpoint.

nodes.title: Fine-tuning & LoRA
nodes.summary: Fine-tuning starts with pretrained weights and adapts them to a task. LoRA trains low-rank updates to selected matrices. Smaller trainable parameter counts do not eliminate activation memory or data-quality requirements.
nodes.question: Does LoRA mean the model needs no GPU or no base weights?
nodes.answer: No. Base weights still participate in computation, and activations use memory. Hardware feasibility depends on model, precision, context, batch size and implementation.
nodes.project: Design a small adapter comparison against the unchanged model using a held-out task set.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Design a small adapter comparison against the unchanged model using a held-out task set.

nodes.title: Reinforcement learning
nodes.summary: An agent learns behavior from rewards over interactions. Credit assignment and exploration differ from supervised target prediction. A reward function can reward unintended shortcuts.
nodes.question: Why is a high reward not automatically evidence of desirable behavior?
nodes.answer: The reward may omit important goals or be exploitable. Test actual task outcomes and side effects independently of the optimized score.
nodes.project: Simulate a small bandit and compare greedy and exploratory action selection.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Simulate a small bandit and compare greedy and exploratory action selection.

nodes.title: RLHF, preferences & alignment
nodes.summary: RLHF often uses preference data and a learned reward with policy optimization. Preference methods such as DPO offer a different training approach. Alignment is broader than one reward or tuning recipe.
nodes.question: Is DPO the same procedure as PPO with an explicit learned reward model?
nodes.answer: No. DPO optimizes a preference objective directly relative to a reference policy; PPO-based RLHF typically includes reward modeling and policy optimization. Neither guarantees safety.
nodes.project: Diagram SFT, reward-model/PPO and direct-preference workflows, including evaluation and data limits.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Diagram SFT, reward-model/PPO and direct-preference workflows, including evaluation and data limits.

nodes.title: Quantization & model memory
nodes.summary: Lower-precision weights can reduce storage and memory. Total runtime memory also includes activations, KV cache and runtime overhead. Compare quality and latency with fixed settings.
nodes.question: Why can a model fail to fit even when its weight file is smaller than available RAM?
nodes.answer: The loaded model needs additional memory for caches, buffers, activations and the runtime. Context and batch size can increase those requirements.
nodes.project: Estimate weight memory for a toy parameter count, then list runtime costs excluded from the estimate.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Estimate weight memory for a toy parameter count, then list runtime costs excluded from the estimate.

nodes.title: Inference & training optimization
nodes.summary: Profile before optimizing. KV caching avoids recomputing previous keys and values during autoregressive inference; attention kernels and batching change throughput and memory tradeoffs. Training has a different workload.
nodes.question: Why can a longer context increase memory even with quantized weights?
nodes.answer: Attention state and KV caches grow with sequence length and batch size. Weight compression does not automatically compress all runtime state.
nodes.project: Measure latency on a fixed workload at two context sizes and separate prefill from generation.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Measure latency on a fixed workload at two context sizes and separate prefill from generation.

nodes.title: Scaling laws & compute budgets
nodes.summary: Empirical scaling laws describe relationships among loss, model size, data and compute within studied settings. They guide budgets but are not universal guarantees for every architecture or task.
nodes.question: Why is an observed power-law trend not a guarantee for an arbitrary model?
nodes.answer: It is an empirical fit over particular experiments. Data quality, architecture, optimization and regime changes can invalidate extrapolation.
nodes.project: Plot a hypothetical loss-versus-compute curve and label measured points separately from extrapolations.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Plot a hypothetical loss-versus-compute curve and label measured points separately from extrapolations.

nodes.title: Distributed training
nodes.summary: Data, tensor and pipeline parallelism split different parts of the workload. Communication, synchronization and failures affect scaling. Study on diagrams or tiny processes before needing multiple GPUs.
nodes.question: How do data and tensor parallelism differ?
nodes.answer: Data parallel workers process different batches with replicated model parameters and synchronize gradients. Tensor parallelism partitions tensor computations or parameters across workers.
nodes.project: Draw two-worker data parallelism and identify where gradients synchronize and communication costs arise.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Draw two-worker data parallelism and identify where gradients synchronize and communication costs arise.

nodes.title: Laptop, Android & Pi delivery
nodes.summary: Run experiments on the laptop, use Android for cached reading and downloaded audio, and use a confirmed Pi model for lightweight serving. Device capability is measured, not inferred from a marketing name.
nodes.question: Why does opening localhost on Android not connect to the laptop?
nodes.answer: Localhost refers to the device running the browser. Use a deliberately configured network service or copy static files/audio; the local model bridge here is loopback-only.
nodes.project: Copy one WAV and transcript to Android; test playback with screen locked and record device details.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Copy one WAV and transcript to Android; test playback with screen locked and record device details.

nodes.title: SQL: filter, group and join
nodes.summary: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY with HAVING, CASE, NULL handling and the four joins. Every later step reads or writes SQL, and an anti join (rows with no match) is how orphans are found.
nodes.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING, and between an inner and a left join?
nodes.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. An inner join keeps only matching pairs; a left join keeps every left row and fills the right side with NULL when nothing matches, which is how rows without a match are found.
nodes.project: Solve the SQL filter, group and join exercises, then write a query listing customers with no accounts.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Solve the SQL filter, group and join exercises, then write a query listing customers with no accounts.

nodes.title: SQL window functions
nodes.summary: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD and running sums compute over related rows without collapsing them. They deduplicate (first row per key), build SCD versions and answer most analysis questions.
nodes.question: How do you keep only the first loaded row per key with a window function?
nodes.answer: Number the rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY load_id) in a CTE, then keep rn = 1 outside it. A window function cannot be used in WHERE directly.
nodes.project: Solve the window function exercises, then deduplicate a table of repeated rows keeping the earliest.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Solve the window function exercises, then deduplicate a table of repeated rows keeping the earliest.

nodes.title: Contracts and profiling
nodes.summary: A data contract states what the source promises; a profile compares the data with it before anything is transformed. Read as text, count missing and distinct values, find repeated keys and orphans. Step 1 of the project.
nodes.question: Why profile raw files with every column read as text?
nodes.answer: Type inference changes data silently: zip codes lose leading zeros and unparseable values become NULL. Text shows the raw values, so every problem is visible and gets an explicit rule later.
nodes.project: Run generate and profile in the ETL project and explain three differences between the profile and _manifest.json.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run generate and profile in the ETL project and explain three differences between the profile and _manifest.json.

nodes.title: Keys, grain and normal forms
nodes.summary: Primary and foreign keys, the grain of a table, fan-out when two child tables are joined, and normalisation to 3NF through functional dependencies.
nodes.question: An order has two lines and one payment. What goes wrong when you join lines to payments and sum payments, and how do you fix it?
nodes.answer: Fan-out: the payment is paired with both lines and counted twice. Aggregate each table to one row per order first, then join.
nodes.project: Draw the 3NF schema of the seven Olist tables with every key, and name the grain of each table.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Draw the 3NF schema of the seven Olist tables with every key, and name the grain of each table.

nodes.title: Docker and Compose
nodes.summary: Images, containers, volumes and Compose services with health checks and profiles, so Postgres, the pipeline, Airflow, Kafka and the dashboard run the same everywhere.
nodes.question: Why does the pipeline container connect to host postgres instead of localhost?
nodes.answer: Inside a container localhost is the container itself. Compose services reach each other by service name on the project network; localhost:5432 only works from the host through the published port.
nodes.project: Start Postgres with docker compose, connect with psql or pgAdmin, and run the pipeline once with docker compose run.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Start Postgres with docker compose, connect with psql or pgAdmin, and run the pipeline once with docker compose run.

nodes.title: Loading Postgres: raw, then core
nodes.summary: COPY the files into text-only raw tables, then build typed core tables in SQL: deduplicate, standardise, validate, reject children of rejected parents, insert under constraints. Each load is one transaction, so it can be rerun. Step 2.
nodes.question: Why deduplicate before validating when building core from raw?
nodes.answer: So the result depends only on the data: the first loaded copy always wins, and an invalid first copy cannot let a later copy through. A rerun then produces the same tables.
nodes.project: Run load-raw and build-core, and explain every difference between the raw and core row counts.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run load-raw and build-core, and explain every difference between the raw and core row counts.

nodes.title: Spark DataFrames
nodes.summary: Driver, executors and partitions; lazy transformations and actions; narrow operations and the shuffle; explicit schemas, ANSI mode and Parquet.
nodes.question: What runs when you chain filter and select on a DataFrame, and which operations cause a shuffle?
nodes.answer: Nothing runs until an action such as count or write: Spark records a plan and optimises it whole. Wide operations (groupBy, join, distinct, windows) shuffle rows by key across executors; filter and select do not.
nodes.project: Read the silver orders with an explicit schema, count late deliveries per month, and find the shuffle in df.explain().
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Read the silver orders with an explicit schema, count late deliveries per month, and find the shuffle in df.explain().

nodes.title: Bronze, silver and quarantine
nodes.summary: The medallion lake: bronze as received, silver typed and deduplicated, quarantine with every reason a row failed. Safe casts, exact duplicates versus conflicting keys, orphans versus children of rejected parents. Step 3.
nodes.question: Why quarantine bad rows with reason codes instead of filtering them out?
nodes.answer: Nothing disappears silently: each rejected row is kept, counted per reason and can be inspected or replayed after a fix. Collecting every reason lets one row count against several checks.
nodes.project: Run bronze and silver and explain the three largest quarantine reasons in the silver report.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run bronze and silver and explain the three largest quarantine reasons in the silver report.

nodes.title: Star schema and SCD Type 2
nodes.summary: Facts at a declared grain, dimensions around them, surrogate keys and an unknown member, and a customer dimension that keeps history (SCD Type 2) joined at the time of each order. Step 4.
nodes.question: A customer moves city. How does SCD Type 2 record it, and how does an old order find the old city?
nodes.answer: The current version gets an end date and a new version with a new surrogate key starts. The fact stores the version key chosen by a point-in-time join, effective_from <= purchased_at < effective_to, so old orders keep the old city.
nodes.project: Build gold and show one person with two versions in dim_customer and an order joined to each.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Build gold and show one person with two versions in dim_customer and an order joined to each.

nodes.title: Data quality as code
nodes.summary: Row-level rules generated from the contract, table-level gates, blocking checks and write-audit-publish, check history, and the precision and recall of the checks against known defects. Step 5.
nodes.question: What is write-audit-publish, and how do you know your checks are good?
nodes.answer: Write the new tables, run blocking gates on them, publish only if they pass, so consumers never see a broken table. Score the checks against ground truth: recall is the share of bad rows caught, precision the share of flagged rows that were bad.
nodes.project: Run quality on synthetic data with two defect rates and compare precision, recall and the quarantine rate.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run quality on synthetic data with two defect rates and compare precision, recall and the quarantine rate.

nodes.title: Analytics SQL
nodes.summary: Business questions on the star schema with CTEs and window functions: growth, shares and Pareto cuts, repeat customers, cohorts and segments.
nodes.question: Why can LAG give a wrong month-over-month growth, and how do you avoid it?
nodes.answer: LAG returns the previous row, which is not the previous month when a month has no data. Join a calendar (date dimension) first so every month is a row.
nodes.project: Answer three of the project's ten questions yourself and compare your SQL with sql/analysis.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Answer three of the project's ten questions yourself and compare your SQL with sql/analysis.

nodes.title: A dashboard on the warehouse
nodes.summary: A Streamlit app on the gold tables in Postgres, with cached queries, a data quality tab, and tests that render every tab in CI. Step 6.
nodes.question: Why build the dashboard as code instead of in a BI tool for this project?
nodes.answer: Code is reviewed, versioned and tested with the pipeline: CI renders every tab, so a schema change that breaks a chart fails the build instead of a meeting.
nodes.project: Start the dashboard with docker compose and explain where every number on the Sales tab comes from.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Start the dashboard with docker compose and explain where every number on the Sales tab comes from.

nodes.title: Spark performance
nodes.summary: Shuffle partitions, broadcast and sort-merge joins, skew and stragglers, adaptive query execution, partition pruning, and a baseline-first benchmark. Step 7.
nodes.question: Which two changes took the project's batch from 176.9 s to 33.0 s, and why did AQE add nothing?
nodes.answer: Sizing spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to the machine (176.9 to 39.5 s) and broadcasting the dimensions (to 33.0 s). AQE coalesces partitions and switches joins at run time, work those two changes had already done.
nodes.project: Run the benchmark and read one stage of the Spark UI: tasks, shuffle read and the slowest task.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run the benchmark and read one stage of the Spark UI: tasks, shuffle read and the slowest task.

nodes.title: Indexes and query plans
nodes.summary: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, sequential and index scans, which keys Postgres indexes for you (primary) and which it does not (foreign), and what indexes cost on writes. Step 7.
nodes.question: A query filters fact_order_line by customer_sk and shows a Seq Scan. What do you do?
nodes.answer: Create an index on customer_sk; Postgres does not index foreign keys. Check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the plan becomes an Index Scan and compare the timings.
nodes.project: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on one customer's order history with and without the gold indexes.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on one customer's order history with and without the gold indexes.

nodes.title: Orchestration with Airflow
nodes.summary: DAGs of tasks, schedules and logical dates, retries, backfills, params, idempotent tasks, quality gates as tasks, and testing a DAG in CI. Step 8.
nodes.question: Why must every task be idempotent, and why do the gate tasks have no retries?
nodes.answer: Retries and backfills run tasks again; a task run twice must give the same result. A failed quality gate means bad data, which waiting will not fix, so it fails at once and blocks everything downstream.
nodes.project: Trigger the DAG with source synthetic, make silver_gate fail, and show which tasks did not run.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Trigger the DAG with source synthetic, make silver_gate fail, and show which tasks did not run.

nodes.title: Kafka: topics, partitions and offsets
nodes.summary: An append-only log split into partitions; keys choose partitions and order holds only within one; consumers track offsets; delivery is at least once by default.
nodes.question: Why are order events keyed by order_id, and what does at-least-once delivery mean for the consumer?
nodes.answer: The key decides the partition, so one order's events stay together and in order. At least once means a message can arrive twice after a retry or a crash, so processing must deduplicate or be idempotent.
nodes.project: Produce 1,000 order events to the local Kafka and read their partitions and offsets with the console consumer.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Produce 1,000 order events to the local Kafka and read their partitions and offsets with the console consumer.

nodes.title: Structured Streaming
nodes.summary: Event time, watermarks, windowed aggregation, deduplication within a watermark, checkpoints and idempotent foreachBatch upserts: exactly-once results from at-least-once input. Step 9.
nodes.question: Which three mechanisms make the stream's results exactly once?
nodes.answer: Checkpoints (offsets and state, so a restart resumes), deduplication by event_id within the watermark, and an idempotent sink that upserts one row per window.
nodes.project: Run produce and stream, then rerun stream and show that daily revenue does not change.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run produce and stream, then rerun stream and show that daily revenue does not change.

nodes.title: Databricks and Snowflake
nodes.summary: The same Spark job on Databricks, the gold tables loaded into Snowflake through a stage and COPY INTO, and what changes in the cloud: secrets, cost and table formats. Step 10.
nodes.question: What has to change in the PySpark transformations to run them on Databricks?
nodes.answer: Almost nothing: the transformations are functions of a session and a lake location. The entry point, the storage paths (volumes or tables) and the credentials change.
nodes.project: Run the Databricks notebook on a sample, or explain each line of the Snowflake load script.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run the Databricks notebook on a sample, or explain each line of the Snowflake load script.

nodes.title: The whole pipeline, explained
nodes.summary: Run everything, defend every number with its data, command, machine and date, and tell one story per step: the problem, the decision, the measurement and what you would change.
nodes.question: In two minutes: what does the pipeline do, and which number are you proudest of and why should anyone believe it?
nodes.answer: Batch and streaming paths from raw files and Kafka to a tested star schema, gated by 115 checks, orchestrated by Airflow. A number is believable when RESULTS.md gives its data, command, machine and date, and you can rerun it.
nodes.project: Run the full pipeline in Docker, fill one story per step in STORIES.md and explain three rows of RESULTS.md.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run the full pipeline in Docker, fill one story per step in STORIES.md and explain three rows of RESULTS.md.

nodes.title: Chunking documents for retrieval
nodes.summary: Split documents on paragraph, then sentence, boundaries into ~800-character chunks with a 120-character overlap, and keep the source file and position with every chunk.
nodes.question: Why split on paragraphs first, and why carry an overlap from one chunk into the next?
nodes.answer: A chunk cut mid-sentence embeds badly and gives the model a broken thought; paragraphs are natural units. The overlap keeps a fact that sits on a boundary retrievable from either side.
nodes.project: Run chunk_text on one document with chunk_size 400 and 800, count the chunks and explain where each boundary fell.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run chunk_text on one document with chunk_size 400 and 800, count the chunks and explain where each boundary fell.

nodes.title: Cosine similarity and exact vector search
nodes.summary: Normalise every vector once at insert time, so cosine similarity is a dot product; score all chunks with one matrix-vector product and take the top k with argpartition.
nodes.question: When is brute-force search the right choice, and when do you need an ANN index such as HNSW?
nodes.answer: For thousands of chunks, a NumPy dot product is exact and takes milliseconds with no extra service. It is O(n) per query, so at hundreds of thousands to millions of vectors an approximate index trades a little recall for sub-linear time.
nodes.project: Add 3 vectors to VectorStore by hand, query with a fourth and verify the order of scores by computing the cosines yourself.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Add 3 vectors to VectorStore by hand, query with a fourth and verify the order of scores by computing the cosines yourself.

nodes.title: Grounded answers with citations
nodes.summary: Retrieve the top-k chunks, number them in the prompt with their source, and instruct the model to answer only from them, cite [n] after every claim and say so when the context is not enough.
nodes.question: What does the system prompt in rag_chain.py do against hallucination, and what can it not guarantee?
nodes.answer: It restricts the answer to numbered context, demands a citation per claim and permits 'I don't know'. It lowers hallucination but cannot prevent it; only a verifier or critic step checks the answer against the sources.
nodes.project: Ask one question the corpus answers and one it does not; show that the second gets an 'not enough information' answer with the mock and a real backend.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Ask one question the corpus answers and one it does not; show that the second gets an 'not enough information' answer with the mock and a real backend.

nodes.title: A ReAct agent loop with safe tools
nodes.summary: An agent is a prompt listing tools and a reply format, a loop that asks the model for its next step, a regex parser for Action and Final Answer, and code that runs the tool and appends the Observation. The calculator parses with ast, so model output can never run code.
nodes.question: Why does the calculator evaluate an ast tree instead of calling eval on the model's text?
nodes.answer: The expression comes from model output, which can be manipulated. Walking the AST and allowing only numbers and + - * / ** makes running arbitrary code impossible; anything else raises an error that goes back as an observation.
nodes.project: Trace run_agent for 'What is 1722 * 2 + 8?' with the scripted fake LLM from tests/test_agent.py and write down every step of the transcript.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Trace run_agent for 'What is 1722 * 2 + 8?' with the scripted fake LLM from tests/test_agent.py and write down every step of the transcript.

nodes.title: Retrieval evaluation: hit rate and MRR
nodes.summary: Twelve hand-labelled questions, each with the document that should be retrieved; hit_rate@k counts questions whose document is in the top k, MRR@k averages 1/rank of the first correct chunk.
nodes.question: The TF-IDF backend already reaches hit_rate@3 = 1.00. What does that tell you, and what does it not?
nodes.answer: On six small, topically distinct documents keyword overlap separates them well, so TF-IDF is a strong baseline here. It does not show how either backend handles paraphrases, synonyms or a large overlapping corpus, which is where dense embeddings pay off; the set is also too small to separate them.
nodes.project: Write three paraphrased questions with no shared keywords, add them to eval_questions.json and compare TF-IDF against sentence-transformers.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Write three paraphrased questions with no shared keywords, add them to eval_questions.json and compare TF-IDF against sentence-transformers.

nodes.title: Pluggable backends, FastAPI and zero-cost tests
nodes.summary: Embedders (sentence-transformers or TF-IDF) and LLMs (OpenAI, Anthropic or a deterministic mock) sit behind small interfaces chosen by configuration, so the whole pipeline is tested offline and served by FastAPI at /health and /query.
nodes.question: Why does every component have a real and an offline implementation?
nodes.answer: Tests then check the pipeline's logic without an API key, network, GPU or model download, so they run anywhere, for free, in CI. Swapping a backend changes configuration, not code.
nodes.project: Run the test suite with LLM_BACKEND=mock, then call /query with curl and explain each field of the response.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run the test suite with LLM_BACKEND=mock, then call /query with curl and explain each field of the response.

nodes.title: The RAG assistant, explained
nodes.summary: Defend every design choice of auto-rag-assistant in an interview: chunking, exact search, the grounding prompt, two agents, evaluation numbers and their limits, and what you would add next.
nodes.question: In two minutes: what does the assistant do, which number are you proudest of, and what is its biggest weakness?
nodes.answer: Chunk, embed and search a small engineering corpus exactly, answer with citations, and let an agent pick retrieval or a calculator. hit_rate@3 and MRR@3 are 1.00 on 12 questions, which is honest only with the caveat that the set is small and keyword-friendly; the next step is a larger, paraphrased set and an answer-level check.
nodes.project: Run build_index, eval_retrieval and the API end to end, and write the three-sentence pitch and the limitation in your own words.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run build_index, eval_retrieval and the API end to end, and write the three-sentence pitch and the limitation in your own words.

nodes.title: FedAvg: averaging models, not data
nodes.summary: Each round the server sends the global weights, every client trains locally for a few epochs on its own data, and the server replaces the global model with the average of the client models weighted by their number of examples.
nodes.question: Why weight the average by each client's number of examples?
nodes.answer: FedAvg approximates training on the union of all data; a client with 300 samples should move the model three times as much as one with 100. An unweighted mean lets small or noisy clients dominate.
nodes.project: By hand, average two clients' weight vectors with 300 and 100 samples, then check it against the train_loss aggregation in fl_server.py.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: By hand, average two clients' weight vectors with 300 and 100 samples, then check it against the train_loss aggregation in fl_server.py.

nodes.title: A Flower server and NumPy clients
nodes.summary: The server subclasses FedAvg to log every round and aggregates metrics with weighted means; each vehicle is a NumPyClient with get_parameters, fit (load weights, train 3 epochs, return weights and sample count) and evaluate.
nodes.question: What must a NumPyClient return from fit, and what does the server do with each part?
nodes.answer: The updated weights as NumPy arrays, the number of training examples and a metrics dict. The server averages the weights by example count and passes the metrics to fit_metrics_aggregation_fn, which here computes a weighted train_loss.
nodes.project: Start the server with MIN_CLIENTS=2 and two lite clients in Docker Compose, then read one round's log line by line.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Start the server with MIN_CLIENTS=2 and two lite clients in Docker Compose, then read one round's log line by line.

nodes.title: gRPC between the server and the fleet
nodes.summary: Flower moves weights over gRPC: a long-lived HTTP/2 connection with binary protobuf messages. Clients dial fl-server:8080; the server waits until min_available_clients have connected before a round starts.
nodes.question: Why gRPC rather than REST for shipping model weights every round?
nodes.answer: Weights are large binary arrays sent repeatedly; protobuf over HTTP/2 is compact, typed and keeps one connection open with streaming, while JSON over REST would base64-inflate the arrays and reconnect each time. The same reasoning drove the KPIT telemetry bridge.
nodes.project: Stop one client mid-training and read what the server logs as failures in aggregate_fit.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Stop one client mid-training and read what the server logs as failures in aggregate_fit.

nodes.title: A heterogeneous fleet with Docker Compose
nodes.summary: Compose puts the server, a ROS2 vehicle and a lite vehicle on one bridge network; the Raspberry Pi joins bare-metal on aarch64 with its own requirements, and MIN_CLIENTS goes from 2 to 3 when it does.
nodes.question: What changes when one client is an aarch64 Raspberry Pi instead of another x86-64 container?
nodes.answer: Wheels must exist for arm64 (hence rpi_requirements.txt and the extract_wheels script), training is slower so rounds wait for the slowest client, and the Pi reaches the server by the host's address, not the Compose service name.
nodes.project: Bring up the stack with run_all.sh, add the Pi with MIN_CLIENTS=3 and time one round with and without it.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Bring up the stack with run_all.sh, add the Pi with MIN_CLIENTS=3 and time one round with and without it.

nodes.title: From ROS2 topics to training features
nodes.summary: A thread-safe buffer collects speed and brake messages from ROS2 topics (last 300 samples) and builds a 12-feature matrix with derived signals such as acceleration from np.gradient; when ROS2 is missing or data is short, the client falls back to synthetic data.
nodes.question: Why a lock around the sensor buffer, and what is the risk of the synthetic fallback?
nodes.answer: The ROS2 callback thread appends while the Flower thread reads features; without a lock a read can see half-updated lists. The fallback keeps a round alive, but a client training on random data adds noise to the global model, so it must be logged and counted, not silent.
nodes.project: Publish speed and brake at 10 Hz with ros2 topic pub and confirm the client switches from synthetic to real features.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Publish speed and brake at 10 Hz with ros2 topic pub and confirm the client switches from synthetic to real features.

nodes.title: Non-IID clients and honest evaluation
nodes.summary: Vehicles see different data distributions, which makes local models drift apart and FedAvg slower or biased. Evaluation must use held-out real data per client; a client that returns a fixed accuracy makes the aggregated metric meaningless.
nodes.question: fl_client.py's evaluate returns accuracy 0.5 for every round. What does that do to the server's weighted accuracy?
nodes.answer: It pins that client's contribution at 0.5, so the aggregate mixes a real number with a constant and cannot show learning. Evaluate on a held-out split of the client's own data, or leave the client out of evaluation.
nodes.project: Give two clients different label distributions, run 5 rounds and plot each client's accuracy against the global one.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Give two clients different label distributions, run 5 rounds and plot each client's accuracy against the global one.

nodes.title: The federated testbed, explained
nodes.summary: Explain the testbed end to end for the minor-project review and interviews: FedAvg, Flower roles, gRPC, a mixed x86-64 and aarch64 fleet, ROS2 features, and what is still synthetic.
nodes.question: In two minutes: what does the testbed show, and what would make its numbers credible?
nodes.answer: A gRPC server runs FedAvg over three heterogeneous clients, containerised and bare-metal, with features from vehicle topics. Credible numbers need real held-out evaluation on every client, logged rounds, and a comparison with centralised training on the same data.
nodes.project: Replace the fixed evaluate with a held-out split, run 5 rounds on 3 clients and record loss and accuracy per round.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Replace the fixed evaluate with a held-out split, run 5 rounds on 3 clients and record loss and accuracy per round.

nodes.title: A leak-free scikit-learn pipeline
nodes.summary: ColumnTransformer imputes (median for numbers, most frequent for categories), scales and one-hot encodes; the target becomes binary (num > 0); the split is stratified and the preprocessing is fitted on training data only.
nodes.question: Why put imputation and scaling inside the Pipeline instead of applying them to the whole dataset first?
nodes.answer: Fitting the imputer or scaler on all rows leaks test-set statistics into training and inflates the score. Inside the Pipeline they are fitted on the training fold only and replayed on the test fold.
nodes.project: Score logistic regression with preprocessing fitted on all data and inside the pipeline; report both and explain the gap.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Score logistic regression with preprocessing fitted on all data and inside the pipeline; report both and explain the gap.

nodes.title: Stratified CV, precision, recall and F1
nodes.summary: Five stratified folds keep the disease rate equal in every fold; for a screening model, recall (missed patients) and precision (false alarms) say more than accuracy, and F1 balances them.
nodes.question: For heart-disease screening, which error is worse, and which metric watches it?
nodes.answer: A missed patient (false negative) is usually worse than a false alarm, so recall matters most; report precision too, because a model that flags everyone has perfect recall and is useless.
nodes.project: Run 5-fold stratified CV, report mean and spread of each metric, and pick a decision threshold that gives recall of at least 0.9.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Run 5-fold stratified CV, report mean and spread of each metric, and pick a decision threshold that gives recall of at least 0.9.

nodes.title: RAPIDS cuML: the same API on the GPU
nodes.summary: cuML mirrors scikit-learn's estimators (LogisticRegression, RandomForestClassifier) on CUDA; the preprocessed arrays are exported once as .npy and loaded by both the CPU and GPU scripts so both train on identical data.
nodes.question: Why export the preprocessed arrays instead of letting each script preprocess on its own?
nodes.answer: Both sides must see byte-identical inputs, or a speed or accuracy difference may come from preprocessing rather than the hardware. It also keeps cuDF and pandas differences out of the comparison.
nodes.project: Train cuML and scikit-learn logistic regression on the same .npy files and confirm their accuracies agree to two decimals.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Train cuML and scikit-learn logistic regression on the same .npy files and confirm their accuracies agree to two decimals.

nodes.title: Logistic regression as CUDA kernels
nodes.summary: Four kernels, one thread per sample or weight: forward (sigmoid of X·w), error (prediction minus label), gradient (Xᵀ·error averaged over samples) and an SGD update; the host copies data once and loops the launches.
nodes.question: What is the gradient of the logistic loss with respect to w, and which kernel computes it?
nodes.answer: ∇w = (1/n)·Xᵀ(σ(Xw) − y). compute_error forms σ(Xw) − y and compute_gradient reduces it with X over the samples, one thread per weight.
nodes.project: Compile host.cu and kernel.cu with nvcc on the V100 or Kaggle, train 200 epochs and compare the weights with scikit-learn's.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Compile host.cu and kernel.cu with nvcc on the V100 or Kaggle, train 200 epochs and compare the weights with scikit-learn's.

nodes.title: Measuring speedup honestly: overheads and Amdahl's law
nodes.summary: With a few hundred rows the GPU loses: transfers and kernel launches cost more than the work. The GPU wins when the work grows (thousands of trees, more rows); Amdahl's law caps the gain by the serial share of the run.
nodes.question: If 20% of a run cannot be parallelised, what is the largest possible speedup?
nodes.answer: 1 / 0.2 = 5×, however many GPU cores you add (Amdahl: S = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/N) → 1/(1 − p)). That is why the honest headline is 'up to 5×' at scale, not '100×'.
nodes.project: Time CPU and GPU random forests at 200 and 10,000 trees with a warm-up run and 3 repeats, and fit p from the two speedups.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Time CPU and GPU random forests at 200 and 10,000 trees with a warm-up run and 3 repeats, and fit p from the two speedups.

nodes.title: The GPU pipeline, explained
nodes.summary: Defend the project: a leak-free CPU baseline, stratified metrics, the same data on cuML, a hand-written CUDA logistic regression, and speedups measured with warm-ups and stated limits.
nodes.question: In two minutes: what did you accelerate, by how much, and when does the GPU not help?
nodes.answer: Training on RAPIDS cuML and in hand-written CUDA kernels, with up to 5× speedup at large model sizes; on a few hundred rows the transfer and launch overhead makes the CPU faster, and Amdahl's law bounds the gain by the serial part.
nodes.project: Rerun the CPU and GPU scripts on Kaggle's T4, record times with repeats in a table, and write the limits next to the numbers.
nodes.outcome: Demonstrate: Rerun the CPU and GPU scripts on Kaggle's T4, record times with repeats in a table, and write the limits next to the numbers.
